What is the geometrical interpretation of the transformation represented by the matrix $A$ given below? 

 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
The rotation matrix ${R}_{\theta }$ represents a rotation of angle $\theta $ counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}],
$$

Comparing $A$ with the rotation matrix, we have 

$$
{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta <0$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta >0$ we must have $\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi .$ 

Dividing the first equation by the second gives

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =-1.
$$

The principal value $\theta $ is

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)=-\frac{\pi }{4},
$$

Therefore, $A$ represents a rotation of $\frac{\pi }{4}$ radians *clockwise* about the origin.

after.worked_solution:
The rotation matrix ${R}_{\theta }$ represents a rotation of angle $\theta $ counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}].
$$

Substituting $\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{4}$ into the above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the image of $S$ under the transformation, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the rotation $R$ by calculating the matrix product $RX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}RX & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{ }[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & -5 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \sqrt{2} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of ${S}^{′}$ are 

$$
(0,\sqrt{2}),\,(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}),\,(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}).
$$

So, the correct answer is "I only."

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}].
$$

Substituting $\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{4}$ into the above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4}) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4}) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the image of $S$ under the transformation, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the rotation $R$ by calculating the matrix product $RX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}RX & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{ }[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & -5 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \sqrt{2} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
(0,\sqrt{2}),\,(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}),\,(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}).
$$

So, the correct answer is "I only."

The rotation matrix ${R}_{\theta }$ represents a rotation of angle $\theta $ counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

$$
{R}_{\theta }=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}].
$$

Comparing $A$ with the rotation matrix, we have 

$$
{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since both $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ are positive, we must have $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Dividing the first equation by the second gives

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =1.
$$

Hence,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

Therefore, $A$ represents a rotation of $\frac{\pi }{4}$ radians anticlockwise about the origin.
